Heat Stroke: Recognizing and Responding Immediately
Health Awareness Reference — General Public Guidance for Odisha's Summer Season
Odisha regularly experiences severe heatwave conditions between April and June, with high humidity adding to the risk. Heat stroke is the most dangerous heat-related illness and is a medical emergency — the body's temperature-control system fails, and body temperature can rise to dangerous levels within a short time. Warning signs include hot, dry, flushed skin with little or no sweating, confusion or agitation, slurred speech, dizziness, a very fast heartbeat, seizures, and loss of consciousness. Recognizing these signs early and acting immediately can save a life.
What to Do Immediately
Act immediately. If you suspect heat stroke, treat it as a medical emergency from the very first sign — do not wait to see if symptoms worsen.
Move the person to a cool place right away. Move the person out of the sun into shade, a ventilated room, or any cooler space, and keep others from crowding around them.
Remove excess clothing. Take off heavy outer clothing so heat can escape from the body; light clothing can remain.
Begin active cooling without delay. Douse or sponge the person with cool (not ice-cold) water, or use wet cloths and towels over the body, re-wetting them frequently. Fanning the person while the skin is wet speeds up cooling.
Apply cold packs to key areas. Place ice packs or cold, wet cloths on the neck, armpits, and groin, where blood vessels are close to the skin, to help lower body temperature faster.
Monitor temperature if possible. If a thermometer is available, monitor the person's temperature and continue cooling until it drops to a safer level; stop aggressive cooling once the person is stable, to avoid overcooling.
Keep the person positioned comfortably. Have the person lie down with the head and shoulders slightly raised.
Give small sips of water only if the person is fully conscious. If the person is conscious, alert, and not vomiting, offer small sips of plain cool water. Do not force fluids.
Call for emergency help immediately. Call emergency medical services (112 / 108) right away and continue cooling efforts while waiting for the ambulance to arrive; every heat stroke case needs hospital evaluation.
If seizures occur, keep the person safe. If the person has a seizure, protect them from injury by clearing the area of hard or sharp objects; do not restrain their movements or put anything in their mouth.
What NOT to Do
Do not use extremely cold or ice-cold water for cooling. Ice-cold water or ice baths can cause shivering, blood vessel constriction, and skin injury; use cool water and ice packs at pulse points instead.
Do not give fluids to someone who is confused, vomiting, or unconscious. A person with confusion, vomiting, or reduced consciousness can choke; only give small sips of water to someone who is fully alert and able to swallow safely.
Do not give paracetamol, aspirin, or other fever-reducing medicines. These medicines do not treat heat stroke and can be harmful in this condition; cooling and emergency care are what the person needs.
Do not assume the person will recover with rest alone. Heat stroke can worsen quickly; assuming rest alone will resolve it can cost precious time.
Do not cover the person with thick blankets or heavy clothing. This traps heat and slows recovery instead of helping.
Do not delay calling emergency services while attempting home remedies. Even after some cooling, internal organ damage may already be underway and requires medical evaluation.
Do not stop cooling efforts too early. Continue cooling measures until help arrives or the person is clearly recovering and alert.
Do not leave the person alone or ignore early warning signs as "just tiredness." Sudden collapse or fainting in extreme heat should never be dismissed as ordinary tiredness.
When to Call Emergency Services
Call emergency medical services (112 or 108) immediately if the person shows any of the following:
Hot, dry, or flushed skin with little or no sweating.
Confusion, agitation, slurred speech, or unusual behaviour.
Very high body temperature (around 40°C / 104°F or higher, if measurable).
A very fast or irregular heartbeat.
Seizures or convulsions.
Fainting or loss of consciousness.
Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down.
No improvement despite active cooling, or the person's condition is worsening.
All suspected heat stroke cases require hospital-level care, even if the person appears to recover after initial cooling, because internal effects on the kidneys, liver, and brain may not be immediately visible. Begin first-aid cooling while waiting for the ambulance rather than waiting for it to arrive before acting.
Source Basis
This document is based on general, publicly available heat-related illness guidance from Indian and international public health authorities, paraphrased in original wording for awareness purposes. It does not quote any source directly.
World Health Organization (WHO) — heat and health guidance
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India — heatwave advisories and National Action Plan on Heat-Related Illness
National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health (NPCCHH) — Training Manual for Community Members on Recognising and Preventing Heat-Related Illnesses, and Emergency Cooling for Severe Heat-Related Illnesses guidance
National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), Government of India — heatwave preparedness guidelines
General public emergency-medicine and heat-illness awareness resources
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
